questions.q: Why does rebuilding an entire table on every pipeline run stop scaling well?
options: It re-scans and re-transforms unchanged historical data every run, wasting compute for no benefit as volume grows
Snowflake tables have a hard row-count limit that CTAS cannot exceed
Rebuilding a table is always slower than any incremental method regardless of data size
Snowflake charges extra for CREATE OR REPLACE statements specifically
questions.explain: At small volume a full rebuild is fine, but once most of the data is unchanged history, re-processing everything every run wastes compute that an incremental approach avoids.

questions.q: What is a watermark (high-water mark) in an incremental loading pattern?
options: The highest value of an ever-increasing column, usually a timestamp, that has already been processed
A visual mark placed on a Snowsight worksheet to flag errors
A Snowflake feature that automatically deletes old data
The name of the warehouse used to run a load
questions.explain: A watermark tracks the highest already-processed value of a column like a load timestamp, so each run can filter for only rows newer than it.

questions.q: What statement applies an incremental batch of updates and inserts in one operation, using syntax already familiar from T-SQL?
options: MERGE
TRUNCATE
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE
GRANT
questions.explain: MERGE matches source rows against a target table and can update matched rows and insert unmatched ones in a single statement — the same core idea as T-SQL's MERGE.

questions.q: What must happen after a MERGE-based incremental load completes, and why?
options: The watermark must be advanced to the new maximum, or the next run will reprocess the same rows
The staging table must be dropped and recreated immediately
Nothing further is needed — the watermark updates itself automatically
The warehouse must be resized before the next run
questions.explain: Forgetting to advance the watermark after a load is a real bug: the next run's filter would still use the old watermark value and pull (and reprocess) the same rows again.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what will Chapter 8's Streams eventually replace?
options: Hand-rolled watermark tracking, by automatically tracking which rows changed since they were last consumed
The MERGE statement entirely, making it obsolete
The need for a warehouse to run any SQL
CREATE TABLE AS SELECT as the primary way to build tables
questions.explain: Streams are a native Snowflake object that automate the row-change bookkeeping a manually maintained watermark table handles by hand — covered fully in Chapter 8.
